c:clock_add_jump_callback.why: time-jump notification -- rcl calls back when the clock steps (simulation reset, NTP correction), with a threshold selecting which jumps qualify. Ours has no notification at all; on a device a monotonic clock does not step, and the simulation case now has ROS time in every language (issue 0789) without anyone asking to be TOLD that the clock stepped -- a simulator writes the time, the nodes read it.

Describes which KIND of change occurred (ROS time activated, deactivated, stepped).

c:clock_get_now_ns.why: rcl's `rcl_clock_get_now(clock, rcl_time_point_value_t* out)` writes through a pointer and returns a status. Ours returns the nanoseconds directly, because a clock read cannot fail once the clock is valid -- the platform seam (RFC-0073) either has a clock or the image did not boot.

This is the ours-only half of `c:clock_valid`; both halves now make the same statement from their own side. No code change.

Ours are `uint64_t` milliseconds at the C API's timer entry points and a `TimerDuration` in Rust -- the unit is named in the parameter rather than in a typedef. This is why the QoS accessors read `deadline_ms` rather than `deadline`; see the qos stage.

c:ros_clock_fini.why: rcl builds a clock per kind through a named init pair (`rcl_steady_clock_init`, `rcl_system_clock_init`, `rcl_ros_clock_init`) as well as a generic `rcl_clock_init` taking a `rcl_clock_type_t`. Ours is the generic form only -- `nros_clock_init(clock, type)` -- because a per-kind entry point buys nothing when the kinds are an enum, and the allocator argument they also carry does not exist.

c:sleep_ms.why: rclcpp's `Rate` blocks the calling thread in a sleep loop to hold a fixed frequency. RFC-0021 forbids a blocking helper that does not drive the executor -- a `Rate::sleep` on a single-threaded executor stops the transport for the whole period. The periodic work shape here is a timer, which the executor drives. rclc's `rclc_sleep_ms` is the same shape. Our platform sleep (`nros_platform_sleep_us`) exists for the BOARD layer, not for application code.

c:time_add.why: `nros_time_add(nros_time_t, nros_duration_t) -> nros_time_t`. rcl has no time addition at all. CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5, group B): the old text offered `only rcl_difference_times` as the neighbouring operation, which reads as though the two were a pair; they are not -- `rcl_difference_times` is Time - Time -> Duration and has no additive form. Ours pairs with `nros_time_sub` (Time +/- Duration -> Time), matching C++ (time.hpp:78/81) and Rust (time.rs:100/109). See `c:difference_times`.

c:time_sub.why: `nros_time_sub(nros_time_t, nros_duration_t) -> nros_time_t` -- subtract a DURATION from a TIME. CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5, group B): this is NOT `the ours-only half of c:difference_times`. rcl's function is Time - Time -> Duration; this one is Time - Duration -> Time, and rcl has no Time - Duration operation under any spelling. c:timer_clock.why:
RE-VERDICTED 2026-09-07 (phase-430 W1). The original reason is now FALSE and is kept below so the change is legible: a timer CAN be created on a clock other than the executor's, via `nros_timer_init_on_clock`, so the accessor would no longer return a constant.

Still declined, for a different reason: rcl's `rcl_timer_clock(timer, rcl_clock_t **)` exists because `rcl_timer_t` is opaque. Ours is not -- `nros_timer_t` is a transparent struct in `<nros/nros_generated.h>` and the clock is the public field `timer.clock` (NULL for a wall timer). The accessor would be a function around a field read, which is the inverse of `c:clock_get_type`'s reasoning and the same answer.

cpp:Node::create_timer.why:
phase-425 W4. The clock-taking timer as a NODE MEMBER: `Result create_timer(Timer& out, const Clock& clock, uint64_t period_ms, nros_cpp_timer_callback_t, void* ctx)` (`node.hpp:557`). Same verb as ROS 2 and the same meaning — bare `create_timer` is the form that takes a clock — but rclcpp humble offers it only as the FREE `rclcpp::create_timer`, whose two overloads take either a `NodeT` or a `shared_ptr<NodeBaseInterface> + shared_ptr<NodeTimersInterface>` pair. We have neither: RFC-0002 puts one executor per RTOS task and there is no interface-fragment layer, so the node IS the receiver. The free form existed too (`cpp:create_timer`, in the since-DELETED `std_compat.hpp`, `NROS_CPP_STD` only — it takes a `std::function` and a `std::chrono::duration`).

NOT a `rename`: the name follows the receiver, and the receiver is the difference — the same reading the graph stage's `Executor::get_node_names` family records. NOT an `extension` either: ROS 2 has this capability, we did not invent it.

`uint64_t period_ms` rather than a `std::chrono::duration` for the reason the whole family gives: a freestanding build has no `<chrono>`. Later ROS 2 distributions add `rclcpp::Node::create_timer` proper; when the recorded surface moves off humble, re-read this row — the receiver argument may stop being needed.

phase-442 W2 (2026-09-11) — `std_compat.hpp` is DELETED, so any sentence above naming that header describes a spelling that no longer exists. It was a third orphaned vocabulary: free functions shadowing the `Node` methods a ported file calls, dead in every shipping configuration, and RFC-0096 removed the layer it belonged to. The always-available spelling is the method.

rename.resolution: Not a rename: this is the name rclcpp uses for exactly this meaning. The name became available when W1 moved our wall timer off it.

cpp:Node::create_timer_in_group.why:

See the pubsub stage's `cpp:Node::create_publisher_in_group`.

phase-427 (the `_in_group` split) -- this row was `cpp:Node::create_timer_in` until the `_in` suffix carried two meanings on one class. `_in` is now the ours-only, storage-free shape only (`cpp:NodeWithTimers::create_wall_timer_in`); a first parameter of `CallbackGroup` takes the longer suffix. RFC-0089, "The `_in` rule, amended".

cpp:Node::create_timer_oneshot.why: a timer that fires once. rclcpp expresses this by cancelling from inside the callback, which needs the timer to be capturable. rust:Executor::register_timer_on_clock.why:
phase-425 W4, and the sibling of `rust:Executor::register_timer` — same receiver argument, same verdict. rclrs expresses the clock choice as a per-site OPTION (`IntoTimerOptions::{steady_time, system_time, node_time, clock}`, all `declined` above) on `Node::create_timer_repeating`; ours is a second registrar on the EXECUTOR, because RFC-0002 puts one executor per RTOS task and it owns the entity arena the timer lives in.

`TimerClockSource::{Steady, Ros, System}` is the argument; a `Ros` timer follows `/clock` when a source is active and reads system time when none is, the same fallback `rclcpp::Clock` has.

cpp:Rate::period.why:
phase-417 W2.d — `rclcpp::Rate`/`WallRate` is a FORWARDER onto `nros::spin(remaining_ms, poll_ms)`, which DRIVES the executor. That is the class's divergence and it lives on `cpp:Rate` and `cpp:Rate::sleep`; this accessor does not sleep, and its own divergence is the RETURN TYPE.

phase-442 W5 / issue 1331 — upstream returns `std::chrono::nanoseconds`; ours returns `nros::Duration` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/nros.hpp:1194`), whose `.nanoseconds()` is the same number `.count()` gave. The reason is the CLASS, not the accessor: `Rate` used to sit entirely inside `#ifdef NROS_CPP_HAS_STD_CHRONO`, so a node written against `rclcpp::Rate` compiled on a host and was ABSENT on ThreadX. W5 measured that the gate was paying for two members out of five and removed it, which means no member may name a type that exists only where `<chrono>` does. Restoring a chrono-returning accessor for hosted builds only would re-create exactly the surface-differs-by-target property W5 deleted.

The porter's edit is one word (`nros::Duration period = rate.period();`) or one call where a chrono type must be kept (`std::chrono::nanoseconds(rate.period().nanoseconds())`). `packages/api/nros-cpp/tests/compile/ros2_api_adoption_stage2.cpp:273` writes the first and says so at the line, so the probe measures our surface rather than adapting around it.

CORRECTED 2026-09-12: the fix that resolved issue 1331 (`9f600be4e`) wrote this paragraph onto `cpp:Rate::Rate` — the CONSTRUCTOR row — and left this one, the row the filing named and the only row whose signature changed, carrying the sleep-shape reason alone. Both rows now describe their own member.

rust:Executor::timer_elapsed_us.why: phase-417 W5.c — a read of the arena's own timer accounting, exposed so the C accessors forward rather than recompute. rclrs puts the equivalents on `Timer`; RFC-0002's arena owns timer state here, so there is no owning `Timer` object to hang them on and they sit on the executor. Returns `Option` deliberately: "not a timer handle" is a different answer from `0`/`false`, which is issue 1008's shape.

c:timer_init_on_clock.why:
phase-430 W1 -- the clock-taking timer verb in C. rcl has ONE init, `rcl_timer_init(timer, clock, context, period, callback, allocator)`, and its clock is not optional; C has no overloading, so a single verb here would have to grow the parameter and break every existing caller. The platform constraint that decides it is the SAME no-allocator/no-runtime-env one that already made `timer_init` a `rule:no-allocator systematic` match: our timers live in an executor arena the caller supplies, so an init is cheap and a second one costs an image nothing but a symbol.

So the pair is `nros_timer_init` (the wall timer -- what every caller has always got, unchanged, and what rclcpp spells `create_wall_timer`) and `nros_timer_init_on_clock`, which takes an `nros_clock_t *` IN RCL'S POSITION: second, immediately after the timer, ahead of the context-carrying `support`. That is RFC-0089's "C takes rcl's spellings" applied to the ARGUMENT LIST, which is the half of the spelling that survives.

The NAME `rcl_timer_init` stays refused, and for the reason `<nros/rcl_compat.h>` sec. 4 already records rather than a new one: `rcl_timer_callback_t` is `void(*)(rcl_timer_t *, int64_t last_call_time)` and ours is `void(*)(nros_timer_t *, void *context)`, so a ported timer callback is a different FUNCTION and taking the name would be a compile-and-differ. Adding the clock does not change that; closing it still needs a decision about what our callback receives.

`nros_timer_t` grew one field, `const nros_clock_t *clock` (NULL = the wall timer), which is what rcl's timer keeps too. Both verbs end at the ONE dispatch `Executor::register_timer_on_clock`, and the clock kind is mapped by the ONE `nros_c::nros_timer_clock_source`, shared with `nros_cpp_timer_create_on_clock` so a `NROS_CLOCK_ROS_TIME` cannot mean one thing in a C image and another in a C++ one. An UNINITIALIZED clock is refused rather than defaulted to steady. Behaviour pinned by `packages/api/nros-c/tests/run/timer_clock_source.c` in `just check c`.

cpp:Timer::cancel.why: `rclcpp::TimerBase` is now an ALIAS of `::nros::Timer` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/timer.hpp:294`; phase-430 W7 deleted the empty base class this row was filed against), so a ported `timer_->cancel()` compiles and reaches the real method. What remains is the widening: `Result` where upstream returns `void`. RFC-0018 forces an error channel and `Result` is `[[nodiscard]]`, so a discarded call warns — loud. Re-verdicted gap -> divergence by the phase-444 ledger truth pass (2026-09-11).

cpp:Timer::reset.why: The `reset` half of `cpp:Timer::cancel`: reachable through `rclcpp::TimerBase` now that it aliases `::nros::Timer`, widened `void` -> `Result` (`[[nodiscard]]`, loud). Re-verdicted gap -> divergence by the phase-444 ledger truth pass (2026-09-11).

cpp:NodeWithTimers::create_timer_in_grou.why:
the callback-group form of `cpp:ComponentNode::create_timer` (RFC-0047); see `cpp:Node::create_timer_in_group` and, for the shape rclcpp passes through options instead, the pubsub stage's `cpp:Node::create_publisher_in_group`. phase-427 W4: `nros::ComponentNode` is DELETED and this row moved onto the merged `nros::Node`. ComponentNode WRAPPED a node (RFC-0044 Q1 chose wrap over derive), so a component was not a `Node` and every verb had to be forwarded; the merged type IS one.

phase-427 (the `_in_group` split) -- was `cpp:NodeWithTimers::create_timer_in`. This is the overload that made the split necessary on this type: it is pool-parked (storage-free, which `_in` had come to mean) AND takes a group, so one name could not say which family a call had joined. Its sibling `create_wall_timer_in` keeps the short suffix and takes no group. RFC-0089, "The `_in` rule, amended".

cpp:NodeWithTimers::create_wall_timer_in.why:
rclcpp's `Node::create_wall_timer(period, callback)` on the RFC-0044 base: ours is `create_wall_timer<Self, &Self::tick>(period_ms)`, the member bound at compile time for the reason `cpp:ComponentNode::create_subscription` gives, plus a `(period_ms, nros_cpp_timer_callback_t, void* ctx)` escape hatch for non-member handlers. The NAME half of the pair is already recorded: `cpp:Node::create_wall_timer` (rename -- ours should carry rclcpp's name) and `cpp:Node::create_timer` (its ours-only half); this row is that same pair one type over, and the type name is the additional question (`cpp:ComponentNode`). Ours also takes `uint64_t period_ms` rather than a `std::chrono::duration` -- freestanding builds have no `<chrono>`, and the chrono spelling exists as the free `nros::create_timer` under `NROS_CPP_STD` (`cpp:create_timer`) -- and parks the `nros::Timer` in the component's inline pool (`NROS_COMPONENT_MAX_TIMERS`) because there is no allocator to keep it alive in; pool exhaustion sets `ok()=false`.

RENAMED 2026-09-05 (phase-425 W1) with the base: both overloads are thin wrappers over `Node::create_wall_timer`, so they moved with it, as did the macro (`NROS_CREATE_WALL_TIMER`). `create_timer_in_group` keeps its stem. The type name `ComponentNode` remains the additional, separate question. phase-427 W4: `nros::ComponentNode` is DELETED and this row moved onto the merged `nros::Node`. ComponentNode WRAPPED a node (RFC-0044 Q1 chose wrap over derive), so a component was not a `Node` and every verb had to be forwarded; the merged type IS one.

phase-427 (the `_in_group` split) -- `_in` here is ours-only/storage-free and carries no group; the group form on this type is `cpp:NodeWithTimers::create_timer_in_group`.
